ch0.title: Wake Up, Echo
ch0.tagline: A small rover hears something it shouldn't.

intro.text: Good morning, Echo. You are the smallest rover in the Archive, and you have one job.
Beep! Is the job snacks?
No. Since the 1960s, people have left machines all over the solar system. Most were forgotten by everyone except the engineers who built them.
Forgotten? But I can hear them. There is a tiny signal in my antenna right now.
Then let's see if your wheels work. Drive to the three test beacons.

outro.text: Wheels work! Antenna works! And that signal just got louder.
We traced it. It leads back to 1964, to a spacecraft that was built to crash.
Built to crash?! Who does that?
People who needed to know what the Moon looks like up close. Let's go meet it.

ch1.title: Scouts of the Moon
ch1.tagline: Before people could land, robots had to go first.

intro.text: In the early 1960s, nobody knew what the Moon's surface was really like. Some worried a lander might sink into deep dust.
So they sent a robot to look?
They sent Ranger 7. It had cameras and no landing gear. It took photos until the very last second.

middle.text: Those photos helped them pick safe places to land, right?
Exactly. Next came Surveyor 3, which had to land softly. Its engines did not cut off in time, so it bounced twice!
Let me try. I promise to bounce less.

outro.text: Astronauts came all the way back to visit Surveyor 3? That is the nicest thing I have ever heard.
The ground held. The Moon was safe to land on. And that meant people could go next.
People! Wait, I'm getting a new signal. It's so faint. It's almost like light bouncing.

ch2.title: The Ones Who Stayed
ch2.tagline: Astronauts went home. Their equipment did not.

intro.text: July 1969. Two people walked on the Moon for about two and a half hours, and then they went home.
They left all this stuff behind?
Everything heavy had to stay so the small upper stage could lift off. But one thing was left on purpose, and it's still working.
Show me!

middle.text: It has no battery and no computer, and scientists still use it. That's the coolest thing left on the Moon.
Two years later, Apollo 15 brought a car. Astronauts could finally travel far from their lander.
You can follow its route. One rule, the same rule they had: never go farther than you could walk back.

outro.text: I keep thinking about the mirror. Everyone left, and it just kept waiting for light.
It's why we know the Moon drifts away from us, a few centimeters every year.
There's another signal. Much farther away. It's almost too faint to hear.

ch3.title: The Long Way Out
ch3.tagline: How do you reach the edge of the solar system? Borrow a planet.

intro.text: Pioneer 10 launched in 1972. It was meant to last 21 months.
And how long did it actually last?
More than 30 years. It was the first probe to reach Jupiter. Then the Voyager team worked out how to use Jupiter as a giant catapult.

outro.text: So Jupiter throws you, and you never even touch it?
That's gravity. Voyager 2 did this again and again, and it's still the only visitor Uranus and Neptune have ever had.
Now I'm picking up something on Mars. It's very quiet, and it's very old.

ch4.title: First Steps on Mars
ch4.tagline: A robot lands on Mars and asks the biggest question of all.

intro.text: Landing on Mars is harder than landing on the Moon. The air is thin, but it's still there, and it's still in your way.
So is the air good or bad?
Both. Thick enough for a parachute, too thin to stop you. Viking 1 needed a parachute and rockets. It's your turn.

outro.text: So was there life or not?
The soil did something strange, but they found no clear evidence of life. People are still arguing about it.
I like that nobody knows. It means there's more to find out.
Viking 1 worked for more than six years. And then, one day in 1982, it stopped answering.

ch5.title: The Little Rovers That Could
ch5.tagline: Built to last days. They lasted years.

intro.text: Wheels! I hear wheels on Mars! Family!
That's your great-grandparent, Sojourner. It was about as big as a microwave oven, and it was the first rover on Mars.

middle.text: Then came Opportunity. Its planned mission was 90 Martian days. Solar panels gave it power, as long as the sun got through.
I see a trail. And little round stones everywhere. What are they?
Scientists called them blueberries. Follow the trail, watch your battery, and keep an eye on the sky.

outro.text: It was supposed to last 90 days, and it lasted almost 15 years.
In June 2018, a dust storm covered the whole planet. The sunlight faded. The team kept calling for eight months.
Did it answer?
No. But everyone who ever worked on it still remembers. That's why you're here.

ch6.title: Still Out There
ch6.tagline: Not every machine is abandoned. Some are busy right now.

intro.text: These signals are loud! They're talking back!
That's Curiosity. It's been working since 2012 and it's still climbing a mountain.
But look down. Perseverance brought a very small friend to Mars. It was never meant to do very much.

outro.text: Five flights planned, and it flew seventy-two. Why does everyone keep doing that?
Good engineers build for more than they promise. And the machines keep surprising them.
There's one signal left. It's the farthest one. It's taking hours just to reach me.

ch7.title: A Message for Whoever Finds It
ch7.tagline: The farthest thing we have ever made is still talking.

intro.text: This is Voyager 1. It launched in 1977, and nothing humans have built has ever gone farther.
It's so quiet out here. What's that gold thing on its side?
A letter. It's addressed to anyone who might find it, long after we're gone.

outro.text: I found them all. The ones that crashed, the ones that went quiet, and the ones that are still working.
So tell me. Are they abandoned?
Nope. Every one of them changed what we know. You can't forget something that taught you that much.
Then the Archive is complete, Echo. Well done.
Wait. People are still sending new machines, aren't they? Someone is going to have to remember those too.

m1.title: A Forgotten Explorer
m1.tagline: After the astronauts leave, a rover waits under an old banyan tree.

intro.text: Every machine in the Archive has a story. This one is told by the Moon itself.
I am the Lunar Roving Vehicle. Apollo 15. I have been parked for a very long time.
In real life, astronauts drove me. In this story, the Moon lets me remember.
The astronauts left. The dust stayed. I used to count the stars, but I always get the same number.
Then count something new. I am Cuội. I came up here with a banyan tree, long ago.
And I came with him. The tree is still here. So are we.
Are you real?
The Moon has room for more than one kind of real.
I used to drive. Astronauts sat where you are sitting. I carried their tools and their rocks.
Then let us go and look at what you carried. My legs are tired. Your wheels are not.
Drive to the three markers under the banyan tree.

outro.text: You stopped at the end of your mission. That does not mean you stopped being part of the story.
It feels like the story ended without me.
Then we will find the parts that are still happening. Tomorrow, we collect samples.
I will carry the snacks.

m2.title: The First Journey
m2.tagline: Cuội asks for rocks. Every rock has something to say.

intro.text: Lunar rocks are letters. Scientists on Earth have been reading them for more than fifty years.
I carried them. I never got to read them.
Today you will. Four sample sites. Drive carefully.
What if I bring back the wrong rock?
Then we look again. A wrong guess is not the end of a journey.

outro.text: Six samples. I remember the weight of them.
Each one is a page of the Moon's history. Some are older than the oldest rock on Earth.
The astronauts could only walk so far. I took them farther.
And because they went farther, we know more. That is not nothing.

m3.title: What the Moon Tells Us
m3.tagline: Craters are a record of everything that ever arrived.

intro.text: Look at the craters. They are not all the same age.
Big ones, small ones. I drove around them for three days.
Which patch looks older? What would you look for?
More craters. Softer edges. A surface that has been hit again and again.
Good. Observation is science too. Point, look, and write it down.

outro.text: You noticed something today.
It was only looking.
That is how every discovery starts. Someone looks longer than everybody else.

m4.title: The Last Leaf
m4.tagline: One more signal, from an instrument nobody came back for.

intro.text: Do you hear that? A signal, very faint. Older than your wheels.
It is not a voice. It is a heartbeat of instruments.
Something else was left here in 1969. It listened to the Moon, and then it went quiet.
Can we help it?
Not by fixing it. Nobody can do that. But we can find out what it did.
Follow the signal. We will bring a leaf.

outro.text: It stopped sending after only a few weeks. I thought a mission like that would be a failure.
Its data is still being studied. A short mission can leave a long lesson.
So it is not forgotten.
No. It is remembered by people who were not even born when it listened.

m5.title: Find You in the Universe
m5.tagline: A message takes more than fifty years to reach a child's window.

intro.text: The banyan leaf is glowing.
There is a message in it. Not for me.
A last burst of data, drifting for more than fifty years. Tonight it reaches a window on Earth.
A child is drawing a rover. I think I know that feeling.
What would you tell them?
That it was worth it. Even the quiet part.

outro.text: The Moon keeps what we leave behind. The story keeps what it taught us.
Do not worry about the end of a mission. Worry about the end of the remembering.
Then I will remember. To the end of the wheels.
